Posts 01 and 02 studied groups one at a time: their elements, subgroups, cosets and quotients. This post studies the maps between groups and the ways a group can move a set. Homomorphisms explain what quotient groups really are (every quotient is the image of a homomorphism, and every image is a quotient). Group actions turn a group into a counting machine: the orbit–stabilizer theorem, the class equation and Burnside's lemma all come from one idea. The payoff is the Sylow theorems, which let you prove facts such as "every group of order 15 is cyclic" using nothing but divisibility. The chapter closes with the classification of finite abelian groups.
Series map: 00 Integers, Relations & Modular Arithmetic → 01 Groups & Subgroups → 02 Cosets, Lagrange & Quotient Groups → 03 Homomorphisms, Group Actions & Sylow (this post) → 04 Rings, Ideals & Fields → 05 Field Extensions & Galois Theory.

Homomorphism — a map φ:G→H between groups with φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b) for all a,b∈G. The product on the left is in G, the one on the right is in H.
Kernel — ker⁡φ={g∈G:φ(g)=eH}, the elements sent to the identity.
Image — im⁡φ=φ(G)={φ(g):g∈G}.
Monomorphism / epimorphism — an injective / surjective homomorphism.
Isomorphism — a bijective homomorphism. Write G≅H when one exists.
Automorphism — an isomorphism G→G. The automorphisms of G form a group Aut⁡(G) under composition.
Inner automorphism — conjugation by a fixed element: cg(x)=gxg−1.

Let φ:G→H be a homomorphism. Then:
φ(eG)=eH. Proof: φ(e)=φ(ee)=φ(e)φ(e); multiply both sides by φ(e)−1.
φ(g−1)=φ(g)−1. Proof: φ(g)φ(g−1)=φ(gg−1)=φ(e)=eH.
φ(gk)=φ(g)k for every integer k (induction, plus property 2 for negative k).
If g has finite order n, then the order of φ(g) divides n, because φ(g)n=φ(gn)=eH.
ker⁡φ is a subgroup of G and im⁡φ is a subgroup of H.
Property 4 is the workhorse for ruling maps out. There is no nontrivial homomorphism Z/3Z→Z/4Z: the image of the generator would need an order dividing both 3 and 4, so it is the identity.

Homomorphism · Kernel · Image
det⁡:GLn(R)→R× · SLn(R) · all of R×
sgn⁡:Sn→{±1}, n≥2 · An · {±1}
Z→Z/nZ, k↦k mod n · nZ · all of Z/nZ
exp⁡:(R,+)→(R>0,⋅) · {0} · all of R>0 (isomorphism)
(R,+)→S1, t↦e2πit · Z · the unit circle S1
cg:G→G, x↦gxg−1 · {e} · G (automorphism)
Homomorphisms out of a cyclic group. A homomorphism φ:Z/nZ→Z/mZ is fixed by a=φ(1), since φ(k)=ka. The only condition is that n⋅1=0 must go to 0, that is na≡0(modm). The solutions are the multiples of m/gcd⁡(n,m), so there are exactly gcd⁡(n,m) homomorphisms. For n=12, m=18: 12a≡0(mod18) holds for a∈{0,3,6,9,12,15}, which is gcd⁡(12,18)=6 maps.
Common pitfall: "k↦k mod m" is not a well-defined map Z/nZ→Z/mZ unless m∣n. In Z/4Z, 0=4, but 0 mod 3≠4 mod 3. Always check that a map defined on representatives does not depend on the representative chosen.

Theorem. If φ:G→H is a homomorphism, then ker⁡φ is a normal subgroup of G.
Proof. It is a subgroup: φ(e)=e; if φ(a)=φ(b)=e then φ(ab−1)=φ(a)φ(b)−1=e. It is normal: for k∈ker⁡φ and any g∈G,
φ(gkg−1)=φ(g) φ(k) φ(g)−1=φ(g) e φ(g)−1=e,
so gkg−1∈ker⁡φ. ∎
Theorem. φ is injective if and only if ker⁡φ={e}.
Proof. If φ is injective, only e maps to e. Conversely, if ker⁡φ={e} and φ(a)=φ(b), then φ(ab−1)=e, so ab−1=e and a=b. ∎
More precisely, the fibres of φ are exactly the cosets of the kernel: φ(a)=φ(b) if and only if aker⁡φ=bker⁡φ. This is the whole content of the First Isomorphism Theorem in Chapter 2.

Theorem. Aut⁡(Z/nZ)≅(Z/nZ)×, the group of units modulo n. In particular ∣Aut⁡(Z/nZ)∣=ϕ(n), Euler's totient function from post 00. (This post writes Euler's function as ϕ to keep φ free for homomorphisms.)
Proof. Every endomorphism of Z/nZ is μa(k)=ak for a=μa(1) (see "Homomorphisms out of a cyclic group" with m=n). The map μa is a bijection exactly when its image contains 1, that is when ab≡1(modn) for some b, that is when a is a unit. Define Ψ:(Z/nZ)×→Aut⁡(Z/nZ), a↦μa. It is surjective by what was just said and injective since μa(1)=a recovers a. It is a homomorphism because μa∘μb(k)=abk=μab(k). ∎
Example: (Z/8Z)×={1,3,5,7} and each element squares to 1 (32=9, 52=25, 72=49 are all ≡1). So Aut⁡(Z/8Z)≅Z/2Z×Z/2Z, not cyclic. In the other direction, Aut⁡(Z/2Z×Z/2Z)≅S3: an automorphism may permute the three non-identity elements in any of the 3!=6 ways.
Inner automorphisms. The map G→Aut⁡(G), g↦cg, is a homomorphism (cgch=cgh). Its kernel is the set of g with gxg−1=x for all x, which is the center Z(G) from post 02. Its image is Inn⁡(G). By the First Isomorphism Theorem (next chapter), Inn⁡(G)≅G/Z(G). For D4 (order 8) the center is {e,r2}, so Inn⁡(D4) has order 8/2=4.

Theorem (First Isomorphism Theorem). Let φ:G→H be a homomorphism with kernel K. Then K is normal in G and
G/K ≅ im⁡φ,gK↦φ(g).
Proof. Normality of K was proved in Chapter 1. Define φˉ:G/K→im⁡φ by φˉ(gK)=φ(g).
Well defined. If gK=g′K then g′=gk for some k∈K, so φ(g′)=φ(g)φ(k)=φ(g).
Homomorphism. φˉ(gK⋅g′K)=φˉ(gg′K)=φ(gg′)=φ(g)φ(g′)=φˉ(gK) φˉ(g′K).
Injective. If φˉ(gK)=e then φ(g)=e, so g∈K and gK=K, the identity of G/K. A homomorphism with trivial kernel is injective.
Surjective. Every element of im⁡φ is φ(g)=φˉ(gK). ∎
Read it as a factorisation: every homomorphism is "quotient map, then isomorphism, then inclusion", G→G/K→ ≅ im⁡φ↪H. For finite G it also gives the counting rule ∣G∣=∣ker⁡φ∣⋅∣im⁡φ∣.
Worked applications of the table in Chapter 1:
GLn(R)/SLn(R)≅R× (via det⁡).
Sn/An≅{±1}≅Z/2Z (via sgn⁡), so [Sn:An]=2 and ∣An∣=n!/2.
Z/nZ really is Z modulo the kernel nZ of reduction.
R/Z≅S1 (via t↦e2πit): "the real line wrapped around a circle".
Trick: to identify a quotient G/N, do not work with cosets directly. Find a surjective homomorphism out of G whose kernel is exactly N; its target is the answer.

Theorem (Second, or "diamond"). Let H≤G and N⊴G. Then HN is a subgroup of G, H∩N is normal in H, and
HN/N ≅ H/(H∩N).
(Proof idea: H→HN/N, h↦hN, is surjective with kernel H∩N; apply the First theorem.) For finite groups it gives ∣HN∣=∣H∣ ∣N∣/∣H∩N∣.
Theorem (Third). Let N⊆K be normal subgroups of G. Then K/N is normal in G/N and
(G/N)/(K/N) ≅ G/K.
(Proof idea: G/N→G/K, gN↦gK, is well defined and surjective with kernel K/N.) Example: (Z/12Z)/(4Z/12Z)≅Z/4Z. The subgroup 4Z/12Z={0,4,8} has order 3, and 12/3=4.
Theorem (Correspondence). Let N⊴G and π:G→G/N the quotient map. Then K↦K/N=π(K) is a bijection between subgroups K of G that contain N and subgroups of G/N. It preserves inclusion, indices ([G:K]=[G/N:K/N]) and normality.
So the subgroup lattice of G/N is exactly the part of the lattice of G that sits above N.

Theorem (Cayley). Every group G is isomorphic to a subgroup of the symmetric group Sym⁡(G). If ∣G∣=n, then G is isomorphic to a subgroup of Sn.
Proof. For g∈G let λg:G→G, λg(x)=gx. It is a bijection with inverse λg−1, so λg∈Sym⁡(G). The map Λ:G→Sym⁡(G), g↦λg, is a homomorphism because λgλh(x)=g(hx)=(gh)x=λgh(x). Its kernel is trivial: if λg is the identity then g=ge=λg(e)=e. By the First Isomorphism Theorem G≅im⁡Λ≤Sym⁡(G). ∎
Cayley's theorem is historically important (it says the abstract definition of a group loses nothing compared with "groups of permutations") but it is wasteful: it embeds a group of order 8 in S8, of order 40320. Group actions on smaller sets give much better information, which is the next chapter.

Action — a group G acts on a set X if there is a map G×X→X, (g,x)↦g⋅x, with e⋅x=x and g⋅(h⋅x)=(gh)⋅x.
Permutation representation — equivalently, a homomorphism ρ:G→Sym⁡(X), with ρ(g)(x)=g⋅x. The two descriptions are the same thing.
Faithful action — one whose homomorphism ρ is injective (only e acts as the identity).
Orbit — G⋅x={g⋅x:g∈G}, everywhere x can be moved to.
Stabilizer — Gx={g∈G:g⋅x=x}, the elements that fix x. It is a subgroup of G.
Transitive action — one with a single orbit.
Fixed set — Xg={x∈X:g⋅x=x}, the points a given g fixes.

Sn acts on {1,…,n} by σ⋅i=σ(i). Transitive and faithful.
D4 (order 8, the symmetries of a square, notation from post 01) acts on the four vertices. Label them 1,2,3,4 counter-clockwise; then r=(1 2 3 4) and, taking s to be the reflection in the diagonal through vertices 1 and 3, s=(2 4).
The rotation group of a cube (24 elements) acts on the 6 faces, the 8 vertices and the 12 edges.
Any group acts on itself by left multiplication, g⋅x=gx (this is Cayley's action), and on the left cosets G/H by g⋅xH=gxH.
Any group acts on itself by conjugation, g⋅x=gxg−1. Orbits are conjugacy classes cl⁡(x), and the stabilizer of x is the centralizer CG(x)={g:gx=xg}.
The orbits of an action partition X: the relation "y=g⋅x for some g" is an equivalence relation (reflexive via e, symmetric via g−1, transitive via products), and orbits are its classes (equivalence relations are from post 00).

Theorem (orbit–stabilizer). Let a finite group G act on X and let x∈X. Then
∣G⋅x∣ = [G:Gx] = ∣G∣∣Gx∣.
Proof. Define f from the set of left cosets of Gx to the orbit by f(gGx)=g⋅x.
Well defined and injective. For g,h∈G: g⋅x=h⋅x ⟺ h−1g⋅x=x ⟺ h−1g∈Gx ⟺ gGx=hGx. Reading the chain left to right gives injectivity; right to left gives well-definedness.
Surjective. Every orbit element is g⋅x=f(gGx).
So the orbit is in bijection with the cosets of Gx, and there are [G:Gx]=∣G∣/∣Gx∣ of them by Lagrange's theorem (post 02). ∎
Worked example: D4 on the square. The orbit of vertex 1 is all four vertices (rotations reach each one). The stabilizer of vertex 1 is {e,s}: the only non-identity symmetry fixing vertex 1 is the reflection in the diagonal through it. So ∣G⋅1∣⋅∣G1∣=4⋅2=8=∣D4∣. The proof's bijection is concrete here. The four cosets of {e,s} are {e,s}, {r,rs}, {r2,r2s}, {r3,r3s}, and both elements of rk{e,s} send vertex 1 to vertex k+1.
Worked example: the cube. The rotation group acts transitively on faces, vertices and edges. A face is fixed by the 4 rotations about the axis through its centre; a vertex by the 3 rotations about the long diagonal through it; an edge by the identity and the half-turn about the axis through its midpoint. All three counts agree:
6⋅4 = 8⋅3 = 12⋅2 = 24.
This is also the standard way to find the order of a symmetry group: pick an object, count where it can go, and count what fixes it.
Trick: points in the same orbit have conjugate stabilizers: Gg⋅x=g Gx g−1. So all stabilizers along one orbit have the same size, as the formula requires.

Apply orbit–stabilizer to conjugation. The orbit of x is cl⁡(x) and its stabilizer is CG(x), so ∣cl⁡(x)∣=[G:CG(x)], which divides ∣G∣. An element has a class of size 1 exactly when it commutes with everything, that is when x∈Z(G). Splitting G into classes and collecting the size-1 classes gives the class equation:
∣G∣ = ∣Z(G)∣ + ∑i=1k[G:CG(xi)],
where x1,…,xk are representatives of the classes with more than one element. Each term in the sum is a divisor of ∣G∣ bigger than 1.
Group · Order · Class sizes · Center
S3 · 6 · 1, 2, 3 · trivial
D4 · 8 · 1, 1, 2, 2, 2 · {e,r2}
A4 · 12 · 1, 3, 4, 4 · trivial
S4 · 24 · 1, 3, 6, 6, 8 · trivial
A5 · 60 · 1, 12, 12, 15, 20 · trivial
For D4 the classes are {e}, {r2}, {r,r3}, {s,r2s}, {rs,r3s}. In Sn two permutations are conjugate exactly when they have the same cycle type; in S4 the classes are the identity (1), double transpositions (3), transpositions (6), 4-cycles (6), 3-cycles (8).

A p-group is a group of order pn for a prime p and some n≥1.
Theorem. If ∣G∣=pn with n≥1, then Z(G)≠{e}.
Proof. In the class equation, each [G:CG(xi)] is a divisor of pn bigger than 1, so it is divisible by p. The left side pn is divisible by p. Hence ∣Z(G)∣=pn−∑[G:CG(xi)] is divisible by p. Since e∈Z(G), ∣Z(G)∣≥1, so ∣Z(G)∣≥p. ∎
Lemma. If G/Z(G) is cyclic, then G is abelian.
Proof. Let gZ(G) generate G/Z(G). Every element of G has the form giz with z∈Z(G). Two such elements commute: giz⋅gjw=gi+jzw=gjw⋅giz, since z,w commute with everything. ∎
Corollary. Every group of order p2 is abelian, hence isomorphic to Z/p2Z or Z/pZ×Z/pZ.
Proof. ∣Z(G)∣ is p or p2. If it were p, then G/Z(G) would have order p, hence be cyclic, hence G abelian by the lemma, so Z(G)=G has order p2: a contradiction. So Z(G)=G. The two possibilities come from Chapter 5. ∎
D4 shows that the corollary stops at p2: it has order 23, is not abelian, and its center has order 2.

Theorem (Burnside's lemma, also called the Cauchy–Frobenius lemma). If a finite group G acts on a finite set X, the number of orbits is
#orbits = 1∣G∣∑g∈G∣Xg∣,
the average number of points fixed by an element.
Proof. Count the pairs (g,x) with g⋅x=x in two ways. By g first: ∑g∣Xg∣. By x first: ∑x∣Gx∣=∑x∣G∣/∣G⋅x∣. Group the x by orbits. An orbit O contributes ∣O∣⋅∣G∣/∣O∣=∣G∣. So the total is ∣G∣ times the number of orbits. ∎
The typical use is counting colourings "up to symmetry". If g permutes the positions with c(g) cycles, a colouring with k colours is fixed by g exactly when it is constant on each cycle, so ∣Xg∣=kc(g).
Worked example: necklaces. Colour 6 beads on a circle black or white; two necklaces are the same if one is a rotation of the other. The group is the cyclic group of rotations by 0,1,…,5 steps. A rotation by j steps has gcd⁡(j,6) cycles on the beads: 6,1,2,3,2,1 cycles for j=0,…,5. So
#necklaces=26+21+22+23+22+216=64+2+4+8+4+26=846=14.
If flips are also allowed (the dihedral group of order 12, so "bracelets"), the count drops to 13. With 3 colours and rotations only, the same formula gives (729+3+9+27+9+3)/6=780/6=130.
Worked example: colouring a cube's faces. The 24 rotations of the cube, sorted by type, with the number of cycles each makes on the 6 faces:

identity · 1 · 6
90° or 270° about a face axis · 6 · 3 (two

Worked example: colouring a cube's faces. The 24 rotations of the cube, sorted by type, with the number of cycles each makes on the 6 faces:
Rotation type · How many · Cycles on faces
identity · 1 · 6
90° or 270° about a face axis · 6 · 3 (two fixed faces, one 4-cycle)

With 3 colours:
36+6⋅33+3⋅34+8⋅32+6⋅3324=729+162+243+72+16224=136824=57.
With 2 colours the same table gives (64+48+48+32+48)/24=240/24=10.
Common pitfall: dividing the number of colourings by ∣G∣ (36/24 is not even an integer) is wrong because symmetric colourings have smaller orbits. Burnside's average of fixed points corrects for exactly this.

Lagrange's theorem says the order of a subgroup divides ∣G∣. The converse is false: A4 has order 12 but no subgroup of order 6. The theorems in this chapter recover as much of the converse as is true, for prime powers.

Sylow p-subgroup — if ∣G∣=pkm with p prime and p∤m, a subgroup of order exactly pk (the largest power of p allowed by Lagrange).
np — the number of Sylow p-subgroups of G.
Normalizer — NG(H)={g:gHg−1=H}, the stabilizer of H when G acts on its subgroups by conjugation.
Simple group — a nontrivial group whose only normal subgroups are {e} and itself (post 02).

Theorem (Cauchy). If a prime p divides ∣G∣, then G has an element of order p.
(A short proof, due to McKay, lets Z/pZ rotate the p-tuples (g1,…,gp) with g1g2⋯gp=e and counts fixed points modulo p.)
Theorem (Sylow). Let ∣G∣=pkm with p prime, k≥1 and p∤m.
Existence. G has a subgroup of order pk. More generally, every p-subgroup of G is contained in some Sylow p-subgroup.
Conjugacy. Any two Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate: if P,Q are Sylow, then Q=gPg−1 for some g∈G.
Counting. np≡1(modp), and np divides m. Moreover np=[G:NG(P)] for any Sylow p-subgroup P.
Two consequences are used constantly:
np=1 if and only if the Sylow p-subgroup is normal. (Conjugates of a Sylow subgroup are Sylow, and by part 2 all Sylow subgroups are conjugates of one of them.)
When p divides ∣G∣ only once, the Sylow p-subgroups have prime order p. Two distinct subgroups of prime order meet only in {e}, so the np of them contain np(p−1) elements of order p.
Sylow counts in familiar groups (checked by listing subgroups):
Group · Order · n2 · n3 · n5
S3 · 2⋅3 · 3 · 1 · —
A4 · 22⋅3 · 1 · 4 · —
S4 · 23⋅3 · 3 · 4 · —
A5 · 22⋅3⋅5 · 5 · 10 · 6
Every entry obeys part 3: for A5, n5=6≡1(mod5) and 6∣12; n3=10≡1(mod3) and 10∣20.

Let ∣G∣=15=3⋅5.
n3 divides 5 and n3≡1(mod3). The divisors of 5 are 1 and 5, and 5≡2. So n3=1.
n5 divides 3 and n5≡1(mod5). The divisors of 3 are 1 and 3, and 3≢1. So n5=1.
So G has a normal subgroup P of order 3 and a normal subgroup Q of order 5. Their intersection is a subgroup of both, so its order divides gcd⁡(3,5)=1: P∩Q={e}. For a∈P, b∈Q, the commutator aba−1b−1 lies in Q (as aba−1∈Q) and in P (as ba−1b−1∈P), so it is e and ab=ba. Then ab has order lcm⁡(3,5)=15, and G=⟨ab⟩≅Z/15Z.
The same argument proves: if p<q are primes and p∤q−1, every group of order pq is cyclic. (For p=2, q=3 it fails, correctly: S3 has order 6 and 2∣3−1.)

Let ∣G∣=12=22⋅3. Then n3∣4 with n3≡1(mod3), so n3∈{1,4}; and n2∣3 with n2 odd, so n2∈{1,3}.
If n3=1, the Sylow 3-subgroup is normal and G is not simple.
If n3=4, the four subgroups of order 3 contain 4⋅2=8 elements of order 3. That leaves 12−8=4 elements. A Sylow 2-subgroup has 4 elements, none of order 3, so it must be exactly these 4 elements. There is room for only one, so n2=1 and it is normal.
Either way G has a proper nontrivial normal subgroup. A4 is the second case: n3=4 and n2=1, the normal subgroup being V4={e,(1 2)(3 4),(1 3)(2 4),(1 4)(2 3)}.

If ∣G∣=20=22⋅5, then n5∣4 and n5≡1(mod5) force n5=1. So every group of order 20 has a normal subgroup of order 5 and is not simple.
Trick: the recipe for "no simple group of order n" is: list the allowed np for each prime; if some prime forces np=1, you are done; if not, count elements of prime order and look for a contradiction, as for order 12.
Watch out: Sylow part 3 gives only candidates. n2∈{1,3} for order 12 does not mean both values occur in every group; A4 has n2=1, while the dihedral group of order 12 has n2=3.

For abelian groups the story is complete: they are classified by lists of numbers.
Theorem (fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups). Every finite abelian group A is isomorphic to a direct product of cyclic groups of prime-power order,
A ≅ Z/p1a1Z×⋯×Z/prarZ,
and the list of prime powers piai (the elementary divisors) is unique up to order. Equivalently, A≅Z/d1Z×⋯×Z/dsZ with d1∣d2∣⋯∣ds and d1>1, and the invariant factors di are unique.
To go from elementary divisors to invariant factors, write the prime powers of each prime in decreasing order, then multiply across: the largest power of every prime gives ds, the next largest gives ds−1, and so on. This uses Z/mZ×Z/nZ≅Z/mnZ for coprime m,n (Chapter 1).
Counting. The number of abelian groups of order p1e1⋯prer is the product of the partition numbers p(e1)⋯p(er), since each prime's part is chosen independently as a partition of its exponent.
Worked example: order 72. 72=23⋅32. The exponent 3 has three partitions (3, 2+1, 1+1+1) and the exponent 2 has two (2, 1+1), so there are 3⋅2=6 abelian groups of order 72:
Elementary divisors · Invariant factors
8,9 · Z/72
8,3,3 · Z/3×Z/24
4,2,9 · Z/2×Z/36
4,2,3,3 · Z/6×Z/12
2,2,2,9 · Z/2×Z/2×Z/18
2,2,2,3,3 · Z/2×Z/6×Z/6
(Here Z/n abbreviates Z/nZ.) Check one row: for 4,2,3,3 the powers of 2 in decreasing order are 4,2 and of 3 are 3,3; multiplying across gives 4⋅3=12 and 2⋅3=6, so Z/6×Z/12, and indeed 6∣12.
Common pitfall: Z/2×Z/36 and Z/4×Z/18 are the same group (both have elementary divisors 4,2,9). Always reduce to one normal form before comparing.
The same theorem, stated for finitely generated modules over a principal ideal domain, is the structure theory behind the Jordan normal form; it is planned as a later post.

1. How many homomorphisms are there from Z/20Z to Z/8Z? List the possible images of 1.
Solution
A homomorphism is fixed by a=φ(1), subject to 20a≡0(mod8), i.e. 4a≡0(mod8), i.e. a even. So a∈{0,2,4,6}: four homomorphisms, which is gcd⁡(20,8)=4.
2. Show that Z/8Z, Z/4Z×Z/2Z and (Z/2Z)3 are pairwise non-isomorphic.
Solution
Compare the largest element order. Z/8Z has an element of order 8. In Z/4Z×Z/2Z the order of (a,b) is lcm⁡ of the orders, at most lcm⁡(4,2)=4, and (1,0) has order 4. In (Z/2Z)3 every non-identity element has order 2. The maximal orders 8, 4, 2 differ, so no two are isomorphic. (These are the three abelian groups of order 8, from the partitions 3, 2+1, 1+1+1.)
3. S4 acts on the set of its three "pairings" {{1,2},{3,4}}, {{1,3},{2,4}}, {{1,4},{2,3}}. Use orbit–stabilizer to find the order of the stabilizer of one pairing, and find the kernel of the action.
Solution
The action is transitive (for instance (2 3) swaps the first two pairings, (2 4) swaps the first and third), so the orbit has size 3 and the stabilizer has order 24/3=8. It is a Sylow 2-subgroup (a copy of D4). The kernel is the set of permutations fixing all three pairings: V4={e,(1 2)(3 4),(1 3)(2 4),(1 4)(2 3)}. By the First Isomorphism Theorem, S4/V4 is isomorphic to the image in S3, which has order 24/4=6, so S4/V4≅S3.
4. How many ways are there to colour the 4 vertices of a square with 3 colours,

three pairings: V4={e,(1 2)(3 4),(1 3)(2 4),(1 4)(2 3)}. By the First Isomorphism Theorem, S4/V4 is isomorphic to the image in S3, which has order 24/4=6, so S4/V4≅S3.
4. How many ways are there to colour the 4 vertices of a square with 3 colours, up to rotation? Up to all 8 symmetries of D4?
Solution
Rotations by 0∘,90∘,180∘,270∘ have 4,1,2,1 cycles on the vertices: (34+3+32+3)/4=(81+3+9+3)/4=96/4=24.
For D4 add the reflections. The two diagonal reflections fix 2 vertices and swap 2: 3 cycles each. The two reflections through edge midpoints swap two pairs: 2 cycles each. Total (96+2⋅27+2⋅9)/8=(96+54+18)/8=168/8=21.
5. Prove that no group of order 35 is simple, and in fact that every group of order 35 is cyclic.
Solution
35=5⋅7. n5∣7 and n5≡1(mod5): the divisors are 1, 7 and 7≡2, so n5=1. n7∣5 and n7≡1(mod7): the divisors are 1, 5 and 5≢1, so n7=1. Both Sylow subgroups are normal, meet trivially, and commute elementwise, exactly as for order 15, so G≅Z/5×Z/7≅Z/35. (This is the "p∤q−1" criterion with 5∤6.)
6. List the abelian groups of order 36 in both normal forms.
Solution
36=22⋅32, and p(2)⋅p(2)=2⋅2=4 groups:
4,9 → Z/36
4,3,3 → Z/3×Z/12
2,2,9 → Z/2×Z/18
2,2,3,3 → Z/6×Z/6

7. Let G be a finite group and H a subgroup of index n. Using the action of G on the cosets G/H, show that G has a normal subgroup K⊆H with [G:K] dividing n!. Deduce that a simple group of order 60 has no subgroup of index 2, 3 or 4.
Solution
The action gives a homomorphism ρ:G→Sym⁡(G/H)≅Sn. Its kernel K is normal; anything in K fixes the coset H, so K⊆H. By the First Isomorphism Theorem G/K embeds in Sn, so [G:K] divides n! by Lagrange.
If G is simple of order 60 and [G:H]=n∈{2,3,4}, then K is {e} or G. K=G is impossible since K⊆H≠G. So K={e} and 60 divides n!≤24, a contradiction.

Post 04 moves from one operation to two. A ring has addition and multiplication tied by the distributive law; the integers, the integers modulo n, polynomials and matrices are the models. Every idea of this post has a ring version: ring homomorphisms and their kernels (now called ideals), quotient rings, and a First Isomorphism Theorem with the same proof. Prime and maximal ideals then explain why Z/pZ is a field, and the same construction applied to polynomials builds C and the finite fields that post 05 needs.
